analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited soft money to national parties and forces disclosure of election-season broadcast ads.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Sen. John McCain and 35 cosponsors — 30 Democrats and 5 Republicans — the campaign finance bill never received a committee vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban national political parties from collecting or spending "soft money" — unlimited contributions from corporations, unions, and big donors that bypass normal campaign limits. It would bar federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting that money, require disclosure of broadcast ads that mention candidates shortly before elections, stop officeholders from fundraising in federal buildings, ban the personal use of campaign funds, and post campaign reports on the internet within 24 hours. It also raises some individual donor limits and adds a provision letting union non-members opt out of funding union politics.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and ordinary citizens, who would see elections financed by regulated, publicly disclosed contributions rather than unlimited corporate, union, and wealthy-donor money routed through party committees. Small donors and candidates without access to soft-money networks would compete on closer to even terms. The bill would also directly limit officeholders themselves, by barring fundraising in federal buildings, restricting taxpayer-funded mass mailings in election years, and banning the conversion of campaign funds to personal expenses like country club dues and tuition.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits national party committees and their related entities from soliciting, receiving, or spending any money not subject to federal contribution limits and reporting rules — the unlimited 'soft money' channel.

Requires state and local party committees to pay for federal election activity — voter registration drives, get-out-the-vote efforts, and communications mentioning federal candidates — only with regulated, disclosed funds.
Bars federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting or receiving soft money for federal election activity.

Requires anyone spending more than $10,000 a year on broadcast ads naming a federal candidate within 60 days of a general election or 30 days of a primary to file a detailed, sworn disclosure with the FEC, and requires contributions of $500 or more behind those ads to be identified.

Makes it a crime for federal officials, including the President, Vice President, and Members of Congress, to solicit campaign donations while in federal buildings — closing the White House coffee and overnight-stay style fundraising practices.

Bans converting campaign funds to personal use — home mortgages, clothing, country club memberships, vacations, tuition, health club dues — and restricts taxpayer-funded congressional mass mailings in election years.
Requires electronic filing of campaign reports and directs the FEC to post them on the internet within 24 hours, so the public can see who is funding candidates while elections are happening.
Doubles penalties for knowing and willful campaign law violations and allows disgorgement of funds to the Treasury as a remedy.

analysis.who_pays: National political party committees, which would lose the unlimited soft-money revenue stream; corporations, trade associations, and labor unions, which would lose their largest channel for unregulated political spending and face restrictions on corporate- and union-funded election ads; and large individual donors, who would operate under disclosure requirements, though the bill also raises the aggregate amount an individual may give from $25,000 to $30,000 per year. Incumbent officeholders would also bear direct costs in restricted fundraising, franked mail, and personal use of campaign funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: National parties, big corporate and union donors

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the aggregate amount one individual may contribute each year from $25,000 to $30,000 and creates a new $10,000 annual limit for state party committees, modestly increasing what the biggest donors may legally give.

It codifies the Supreme Court's Beck decision, requiring unions to reduce non-member fees for political use on request — a provision labor organizations opposed, attached as the price of Republican support.

The personal wealth limits for Senate candidates are voluntary: a candidate who declares a $50,000 personal-funds spending cap gets FEC certification, but a millionaire candidate can simply decline and spend freely.

By barring corporate and union treasury money from electioneering ads while leaving individual independent spending largely untouched, the bill could push money toward less accountable channels rather than eliminate it — a structural concern critics raised about the approach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: closing the soft-money channel and mandating prompt public disclosure would substantially reduce the influence of the largest donors on federal elections, at a cost to the parties and interests that had built that system. The bill is not perfectly designed — it buys its handful of Republican cosponsors with higher individual giving limits and an anti-union Beck rider, its wealth limits are voluntary, and money blocked from one channel tends to find another. But the main benefit, ending unlimited undisclosed corporate, union, and wealthy-donor money in federal elections, outweighs those defects.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never took it up, so it never reached the Senate floor and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 1999 in the Senate on January 19, 1999, with 27 other original cosponsors including Sen. Russell Feingold.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, where no further action was ever recorded.

Over the two years of the 106th Congress the bill accumulated 35 cosponsors — 30 Democrats and 5 Republicans — but never received a committee vote, a committee report, or a floor vote in either chamber.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees, corporations, unions, and large individual donors who benefited from the unlimited, weakly disclosed soft-money system kept it intact for the rest of the Congress; the soft-money ban did not become law until a successor bill passed in 2002.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big soft-money donors and national parties

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on January 19, 1999 and recruited a bipartisan group of 27 original cosponsors.

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Joined McCain as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Rules and Administration (106th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to and never scheduled any markup or vote on it; a prominent opponent of campaign finance limits.

against.name: Trent Lott
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded votes exist, but the 35 cosponsors split 30 Democrats to 5 Republicans — two-thirds of the Democratic conference versus fewer than one in ten Republicans — so support leaned heavily Democratic with a small bipartisan flank.

industries.note: The bill bans national parties from raising or spending unlimited soft money, which had become their largest funding channel, and requires parties that make independent expenditures to forgo coordinated ones. State parties gain a new $10,000 donor limit and the individual aggregate limit rises to $30,000, but the overall effect is a major revenue cut for the party organizations.

Corporations would lose the soft-money channel to party committees and be barred from using treasury funds for broadcast ads naming federal candidates in the weeks before elections, except through segregated individual-only accounts. Their political spending would become narrower and fully disclosed.

Unions would face the same electioneering-ad restrictions as corporations, and the Beck rider would require them to reduce non-member fees covering political activity on request — a direct hit to union political treasuries written into the bill.

Big donors would face new disclosure obligations and soft-money restrictions, but the bill raises the aggregate annual giving cap from $25,000 to $30,000 and adds a $10,000 state-party limit, modestly increasing regulated giving capacity.

Political ad money keeps flowing under the bill, but stations' clients face new 24-hour disclosure filings and 'stand by your ad'-style requirements, and the bill leaves the underlying broadcast advertising market intact.
